title: The likelihood sharpens
sub: Log-likelihood of a coin's bias after more and more flips.

frames.caption: A coin of unknown bias p (secretly 0.3, the vertical dashed line). After 5 flips with 3 heads, the blue curve is the log-likelihood ℓ(p), shifted so its peak is at 0. The peak, the MLE, is p̂ = 0.60: the sample proportion.
20 flips, 10 heads. The curve is getting narrower. The green bar marks every p whose log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the peak: a 95% likelihood-ratio interval, here 0.29 to 0.71.

60 flips. The orange dashed parabola has the same peak and the same curvature as ℓ at its peak; that curvature, n / (p̂(1 − p̂)), is the observed Fisher information. Near the peak the two already agree.

200 flips: the log-likelihood is close to a parabola. That is asymptotic normality: p̂ is approximately normal with standard error 1/√(Fisher information) = 0.033, and the interval is roughly p̂ ± 1.96 × 0.033. The curvature grows like n, so the width shrinks like 1/√n: four times the data for half the uncertainty. No unbiased estimator can do better asymptotically (the Cramér-Rao bound).
